exploratory.title: Component item post_science_1 as outcome
exploratory.rationale: Shows whether the planned trust effect is mirrored in a separate post-treatment science item.
exploratory.method: Each message arm was compared with the control using the planned model, with a separate post-treatment science item as the outcome.
exploratory.finding: 2 of 32 arm estimates have p<0.05 (estimates range -0.167 to 0.117), a number consistent with chance across 32 tests.

exploratory.title: Heterogeneity of planned effects by Republican identification
exploratory.rationale: Partisanship is the most likely source of differential response to trust messages.
exploratory.method: The arm-by-subgroup difference in the planned model was estimated, comparing Republican-identifying respondents with others.
exploratory.finding: 1 of 32 arm-by-group interactions has p<0.05 (minimum p 0.004), so there is little evidence of heterogeneity by Republican identification beyond what 32 tests would produce.

lit.text: The retrieved literature that bears on the study's hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science can inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general support to testing whether short messages shift public attitudes toward science. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) examine how misinformation affects people and how it can be countered, which is the closest match to a message-versus-control design on trust. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant consideration for an online message experiment of this kind. The retrieved works do not directly test whether messages change trust in science, so there is no clear finding for or against the hypothesis. The main tension is between Lewandowsky et al. (2017), who stress the adverse influence of misinformation and the difficulty of countering it, and the more general optimism of Van Bavel et al. (2020) about behavioural interventions. A relative-to-control design of the kind the study uses can test whether any message moves trust above the pure control.

sections.abstract: Can short, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid. Respondents were randomly assigned to a pure control or to one of 32 messages (videos, images, text, news stories and a values exercise), and trust in science was measured afterwards. Of 11,519 raw respondents, 8,572 passed the screener and 7,803 entered the models. Message 2 (video) lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p = 0.0002) relative to a control mean of 3.685. Message 26 (video) also lowered it, by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos, Messages 12, 15 and 20, showed small positive effects of about 0.06 points (p < 0.05). Other arms were not distinguishable from control. Because 32 comparisons were made without multiplicity correction, and several arms were small, the modest effects should be treated cautiously.
sections.design_notes: The study was registered on OSF, with later amendments covering the assignment algorithm and covariate adjustment. Respondents were US adults from Lucid. Of 11,519 raw respondents, 8,572 passed the screener and 7,803 entered the H1 models, which is also the eligible count. Arm sizes vary widely because assignment was adaptive, from about 116 in some arms to 921 in Message 20 (video). Each message is compared with the pure control, whose mean trust score was 3.685. Tests are two-sided and uncorrected for the 32 comparisons.

results.H1: Message 2 (video) lowered trust in science by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p = 0.0002, two-sided), and Message 26 (video) lowered it by 0.104 (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos were associated with slightly higher trust: Message 12 (+0.064, 95% CI [+0.005, +0.123], p = 0.034), Message 15 (+0.063, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.112], p = 0.012) and Message 20 (+0.063, 95% CI [+0.016, +0.111], p = 0.009). Among the arms shown, the others, including Message 3 (+0.064, p = 0.077), were not distinguishable from control. With 32 uncorrected tests, the three small positive effects in particular are fragile.

exploratory.E1: Exploratory and unreviewed: using a single component item of the trust measure as the outcome, the output reports 2 of 32 arm estimates with p < 0.05, about what chance would produce. Only part of the table was visible, so this count is unchecked here.
exploratory.E2: Exploratory and unreviewed: interacting each message with Republican identification, 1 of 32 interactions had p < 0.05 (minimum p = 0.004). This is little evidence of heterogeneity beyond what 32 tests would produce.

sections.limitations: Thirty-two arms were each tested against control without correction for multiple comparisons, so isolated significant results may be false positives. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals, while others had several hundred. Even the significant effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale. Outcomes were measured immediately after exposure, so durability is unknown. The sample is US adults on an online panel, which may not generalise to other populations. The exploratory checks come from unreviewed code and should not be given weight.

takeaways: Across 32 student-designed messages, none clearly raised trust in science; the effects were small, and one video lowered it by 0.17 scale points (95% CI [−0.26, −0.08]).
In the registered tests, Message 2 (video) lowered trust in science by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001) relative to the pure control.
Three videos (Messages 12, 15 and 20) raised trust in science by about 0.06 points each, with confidence intervals close to zero (for example Message 20: [+0.016, +0.111]).
Caveat: 32 two-sided tests were run without correction, so the smaller effects in particular could be chance findings; the exploratory checks showed nothing beyond chance.

Of 11,519 respondents, 8,572 entered the analysis. Message 2 (video) lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001) relative to a control mean of 3.685. Message 26 (video) also lowered it, by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024]). Three videos, Messages 12, 15 and 20, raised it by about 0.06 points each, with intervals near zero. The remaining arms were not distinguishable from control. results.H1: Message 2 (video) lowered trust in science by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001, two-sided), and Message 26 (video) lowered it by 0.104 (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Among the arms shown, the others were within about ±0.08 points of control and not distinguishable from it. With 32 uncorrected tests, the three small positive effects in particular are fragile.

got_right: Registered the plan on OSF, with dated amendments for the adaptive assignment algorithm and Lin covariate adjustment, and used a pure control (mean 3.685, n = 664) as a common comparator.
Tested a large, varied message set (videos, images, text, news stories, a values exercise) in one experiment, so formats can be compared on the same outcome and sample.
Reported the full arm table with confidence intervals and flagged the 32 uncorrected tests, so the five nominal hits (two negative, three about +0.06) are read as fragile rather than as findings.
Used pre-treatment trust and covariates with HC2 errors and IPW weights to handle adaptive assignment and gain precision.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Adaptive assignment left most arms at about 120-170 respondents against a control of 664. Per-arm SEs of 0.03-0.05 cannot separate a 0.06-point effect from noise, and nothing survives multiplicity correction except possibly Message 2.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Arm n of 116-180 for most messages; SEs 0.030-0.056; Message 12 p = 0.034 and Message 15 p = 0.012, Message 20 p = 0.009 against 32 uncorrected tests.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Thirty-two uncorrected two-sided contrasts, with five nominal hits, are near the expected chance count of about 1.6 at 0.05. Message 2's p of 0.0002 is the only result that would plausibly survive Bonferroni (0.05/32 ≈ 0.0016).
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Five of 32 arms with p < 0.05. Exploratory checks gave 2 of 32 (component item) and 1 of 32 (Republican interaction) nominal hits.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Arms differ in format, topic, length and tone at once, so a positive or negative arm cannot be traced to a mechanism. The student-designed set has no manipulated mechanism such as credibility, emotion or identity.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Arms mix videos, images, text, news stories on a COVID-19 death and a global-warming study, and a values exercise; the three positive arms are all videos, but so are both negative ones.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Trust is measured once, immediately after exposure, and a ceiling is plausible with a control mean of 3.685. Effects of at most 0.17 points say nothing about durability or behaviour.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Limitations: outcomes measured immediately after exposure; largest effect -0.171 on the trust scale.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Roughly 3,000 of 11,519 respondents were lost to screening, and a further 769 to model exclusions (8,572 analysed, 7,803 modelled). This could create selection that differs by arm, and the Lucid panel limits generalisation.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: 11,519 collected, 8,572 passed the screener, 7,803 entered the H1 models.

debates.label: Can brief messages move trust in science at all?
debates.position_a: Short, well-designed messages can shift attitudes toward science, as behavioural interventions did in pandemic response.
debates.position_b: Misinformation and distrust are sticky and hard to counter, so brief exposures produce little or backfiring change.
debates.what_this_study_says: Leans toward b. Effects are at most about 0.06 points positive, and the largest effect (Message 2) is negative at -0.171. Most arms are indistinguishable from control, and the retrieved literature does not test this directly.

briefs.title: Format-matched message factorial with delayed follow-up
briefs.question: Does the video format, rather than message content, produce the small trust gains, and do they persist after one to two weeks?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the design and power causes: it crosses format with content in a few well-powered cells, and adds a second wave to address the immediate-only outcome.
briefs.design_sketch: Take the best-performing content (the Message 15 and Message 20 themes) and the worst (Message 2) and deliver each as video, image and text, plus a pure control. Measure the trust scale and a behavioural outcome, a donation or sharing choice, immediately and again after 10 days. Recruit from Lucid with the same screener and the same pre-treatment trust and covariates, with equal allocation and no adaptive assignment.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of about 0.063 for Messages 12, 15 and 20, with per-observation SD near 1; two-cell contrast at 80% power, ignoring covariate gains.

briefs.title: Replicate the extremes to separate real effects from chance
briefs.question: Are the Message 2 backlash and the Message 15 and 20 gains reproducible, as position a predicts for the gains and position b for the null?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the multiplicity and power problem: a preregistered confirmatory test of 4 arms replaces 32 exploratory contrasts, so the two positions of the debate are discriminated.
briefs.design_sketch: Run Messages 2, 15, 20 and 26 against a fresh control with equal allocation and a pre-specified Holm correction across the four contrasts. Use the same pre-trust-adjusted model. If the gains replicate at about +0.06 and the backlash at -0.10 or worse, brief messages can move trust. If all shrink toward zero, the original hits were chance.

power_target.basis: Observed +0.063 for Messages 15 and 20; the larger Message 2 effect (-0.171) would need only about 550 per arm.

briefs.title: Partisan and platform boundary of the video effects
briefs.question: Do the video effects on trust differ by Republican identification and by a feed-like versus forced-exposure setting?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the missing moderator and sample causes: the one nominal Republican interaction (Message 15, +0.165, p = 0.004) was found across 32 tests and needs a targeted confirmatory test.
briefs.design_sketch: Randomise Messages 15 and 20 and a control, crossed with forced exposure versus embedding in a social feed. Pre-register Republican identification as the moderator and stratify sampling by party. Measure trust with the same scale.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Republican versus non-Republican identification, and forced versus feed exposure

power_target.basis: Observed Message 15 by Republican interaction of 0.165 (SE 0.057); interaction contrasts need about 4 times the main-effect n, sized to an MDE near 0.1.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but as a narrow confirmation rather than another broad screen. Only Message 2's backlash is clearly distinguishable from noise, and the three small gains of about 0.06 points are at the level expected from 32 uncorrected tests. Run the replication of the extreme arms first, since it is cheap and resolves whether any of the gains is real. Then, if the gains replicate, run the format-by-content factorial with a delayed wave to learn about mechanism and persistence. The retrieved literature is thin on this question, so the debate is framed from the study's own question plus two loosely related works.
